utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We'll go briefly into private session to hear any further submissions in relation to a request for protective measures for Witness 382. After that, we'll continue with the cross-examination of the witness who testifies in closed session, so we'll first go into private session then move into closed session after that until we finish the testimony of the present witness. Ms. Loukas, could you please, after we have gone into private session, would you then please make your submissions. It's not yet confirmed on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Nor on mine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is the decision of the Prosecution's motion for protective measures for Witness 382. The motion, which is partly confidential, was filed on the 29th of March of this year. Since the witness was scheduled to testify today, the Defence met the Chamber's request to respond earlier than it was entitled to under the Rules. The Chamber heard the Defence's oral submissions yesterday, the 30th of March. Pursuant to Rules 75 and 79 of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Prosecution seeks an order that a pseudonym be used when referring to the witness in the proceedings and that the witness be allowed to testify in open session with image distortion. The Prosecution also requests that the witness be allowed to testify in private session for those portions of his testimony which are reasonably likely to reveal his identity. In an oral submission made in court this morning, the Prosecution further requested that the witness be allowed to testify in private session for those portions of his testimony dealing with sexual assault. The Defence did not oppose this last request. In the confidential annex to its motion, the Prosecution describes the general security situation affecting the witness. The witness has expressed fear for the safety of his family, both in and outside Bosnia, if it becomes known that he has given evidence before the Tribunal. Among other information provided, the Prosecution notes both the sensitivity of aspects of the witness's testimony and the fact that the witness has been subject to threats of a serious nature. The Prosecution also incorporates by reference its submissions in relation to a recent UNHCR report, as set out in a separate protective measures motion filed on the 11th of March, 2005. That report describes the current security situation affecting persons who have given, or may give evidence before the Tribunal. In its oral submissions, the Defence recalls that the burden rests on the party seeking protective measures to justify why such measures should be granted in each case. The Defence argued that the Prosecution has not provided the detailed reasoning required for a grant of protective measures and thus has failed to establish a sufficient basis for the protective measures sought in this case. The Trial Chamber has stated the law on protective measures in three recent decisions, notably the decisions of the 20th of September, 2004, transcript page 5613 and following; the 9th of March, 2005, transcript page 10192 and following; and the 21st of March, 2005, transcript page 10821 and following. The Chamber notes that the accused has a right to a fair and public hearing and that proceedings before the Tribunal must be public unless good cause is shown to the contrary. To justify protective measures, it must be shown that should it become publicly known that the witness has testified before this Tribunal, there is a real risk, the existence of which is supported by some objective evidence, to the security of the witness or his or her family. Moreover, it must be shown that less restrictive measures would not deal adequately with the legitimate concerns of the witness. The Chamber has considered the submissions of the parties. It finds that in the present case the Prosecution has established that the witness and the witness's family face a real risk to their security if it becomes known that the witness has testified before the Tribunal. The Chamber makes this finding on the basis of the threats addressed to the witness, the present location of the witness and his family members, and the sensitivity of the witness's expected testimony. The Chamber assesses the fear and the risks resulting from these factors in the general context, that is, the climate in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which reportedly remains unfavourable to persons who are resident there or who have family resident there and who wish to fully discharge their duty to testify. The Trial Chamber notes that the witness has requested to be able to give evidence in private session only for those parts of his testimony likely to reveal his identity and those parts dealing with sexual assault. The requested protective measures, that is, pseudonym, image distortion, and partial private session, strike a fair balance between the need to protect the witness and the accused's right to a public trial. Therefore, the Chamber grants the motion. Since we still are in open session, I would like to ask you, Mr. Gaynor, whether you'd like to start with the witness in private session or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can start in open session. We'll briefly go into private session for some details about his background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I take it that the technicians are aware of the fact that face distortion is effective and the face of the witness will not be shown if he enters the courtroom. Mr. Usher, could you please escort Witness 382 into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is being escorted into the courtroom, I would indicate that my legal assistant, Ms. Kelly Pitcher, is just outside doing some further work in relation to other matters in the case but she will be returning at some point while this session continues, and I just wanted to alert Your Honours to that because apparently there is occasionally problems with security about which door to be let into the courtroom and I just thought I'd alert the relevant people to that aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whenever she's kept for more than 24 hours in this building, Ms. Loukas, you'll inform the President of this Chamber so that I can assist in resolving these kinds of matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I should explain to you as well that the exhibits from the last witness, we have not dealt with them yet. The reason for that is that Ms. Philpott is ill today and we are assisted by different representatives of the Registry and I'd rather deal with it when Ms. Philpott is back who has prepared the numbers, et cetera, and I then take it that Mr. Hannis will be informed about it, unless the parties are already aware of objections/no objections so that even in the absence of Mr. Hannis, we could deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's always preferable to have Ms. Philpott here for the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Philpott, certainly, but I was talking about then Mr. Hannis, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness 382, because that's how we will call you. First of all, we would like to inform you that the Chamber just has given a decision in which the request for protective measures are granted, that is, that we will not call you by your own name but will use the pseudonym, Witness 382; that the outside world cannot see your face when you're testifying; and that some portions of your testimony will be given in private session. That means the outside world will not have any knowledge of the content of those portions of your testimony. Before giving evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this declaration is now handed out to you by the usher. I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness 382, please be seated. Mr. Gaynor, you may proceed. I take it, from what I've seen, that Rule 89(F) will be applied as well in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. My proposal is to first of all deal with the pseudonym sheets, a couple of details about his background, and then to submit his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We can do that in open session. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. 382.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. 382, it's Mr. Gaynor who is going to put the questions to you first.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, the first thing we're going to do is show you a sheet of paper with your name and your date of birth, and I'd just like you to confirm with a simple yes or no whether that is your name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Yes, that is my name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd request that an exhibit number be assigned to that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P575 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a couple of details about your background.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: For this reason, I'm going to ask, Your Honour, to allow us to go into private session very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we propose to submit the statement of this witness which he delivered to investigators of this Tribunal, and we submit that pursuant to Rule 89(F). There are some redactions to this statement and we will be asking the witness to expand on several aspects contained in that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, are you also going to tender the other statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It's our intention not to tender the other statement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because in a supplementary information sheet, I saw something about a Bosnian statement, but I took it that you refer to German statement rather than the Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. That was an error on my part. That was the statement which he prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: First of all, I would request that that statement be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P576.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just prior to that, Your Honour, and just prior to Mr. Gaynor proceeding, just before Your Honours came back into court I was in the process of discussing one small redaction of one sentence, one further redaction, and we hadn't completed our discussion, so I'm happy to -- the evidence might proceed at this point, we can discuss that redaction at some other point, but I just wanted to place that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would that prevent Mr. Gaynor from the 89(F)? Mr. Gaynor, you are aware of what --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I think I know the redaction that Ms. Loukas is referring to, and I have no objection to that redaction.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That certainly shortens the matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's try to concentrate now on the witness, because I see that our procedural matters are a bit over his head and I'd like to avoid that this witness gets the feeling that we talk over your head, so we'll come as soon as possible to what you're really here for, and that's for the testimony. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, as -- I will be asking you a few questions and I will be asking you to expand on some matters which are not set out in that statement, but before we come to that point, I'd like to ask you whether you've had an opportunity to review that statement carefully in the past few days. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And is that statement true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I propose now to read a summary of the evidence contained in that statement, for the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps we explain to the witness, or did you do that already prior to his appearance here? Witness 382, since we are not going to ask you all the questions about -- about the information that you have already given in your statement, a summary is made so that the public, who doesn't see your face but who can listen to what is said in this courtroom, knows what your statement is about and therefore is better able to understand any additional questions put to you on those subjects, and that's what Mr. Gaynor is going to do at this moment. Please proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This witness is a Bosnian Muslim from the town of Rogatica in Rogatica municipality. In his written statement, the witness says that following the outbreak of war in Croatia, JNA officers announced to Muslim reservists who had appeared for military exercises that they were no longer needed and were not to participate in any exercises in the future. The witness describes an attempt by a large number of JNA soldiers and officers to seize weapons held by the local Territorial Defence force which had a Muslim commander. He also describes the formation of the local Serb police force, and the distribution of weapons, at night, from a JNA military truck to local Serbs. The witness had known Rajko Kusic as a friend and as a colleague for a number of years before the war. He worked for several years at the same firm as Kusic. The witness says that after Kusic left his job, he became commander of a paramilitary group. In mid-April 1992, the witness met Rajko Kusic. The witness asked him what was going on. Kusic told him that he and the JNA had to defend the Serbian people and Serbian land. The witness saw artillery positions on the hillsides around Rogatica. Around the 22nd of May, 1992, without warning, the shelling of Rogatica began. The shelling lasted three or four hours that day. From a vantage point, the witness was later able to see the areas damaged by shelling and concluded that those who were carrying out the shelling were targeting Muslim areas. Serb areas were not shelled. The witness and other Muslims later fled to the centre of Rogatica town for protection. Along the way, the witness saw APCs and tanks. The witness says that there was no defence of Rogatica. At the beginning of June, 1992, Zivojin Novakovic, a representative of the VRS, made an announcement from an APC. He called upon the Muslim residents of Rogatica to surrender and to proceed to the Veljko Vlahovic school. Novakovic, who the witness knew, told the witness that the town would be cleansed, that they all had to proceed to the school, and that anyone found in the town would be killed. Shells were fired to persuade the Muslims to go to the school. Approximately 200 to 300 decided to go and surrender at the school. On arrival at the school, the witness was taken away for questioning by Rajko Kusic, who appeared to be in command of the camp at the school. The witness and his family were detained at the school for three and a half months. For the first month, the camp held about 400 people who were mostly women and children. Many new detainees arrived, and the camp eventually held about 1.100 people. Many were transported out, and were told that they were going to Muslim territory. While in detention, the witness says that detainees were subjected to serious abuse. During interrogations, the witness was beaten and tortured with pliers. While detained at the school, the witness became aware that many women, as well as girls as young as 13, were taken to other parts of the camp and to other parts of Rogatica where they were raped by military men and policemen. One soldier, who was a driver for Rajko Kusic, told the witness that Serb soldiers were competing to see how many detainees they could rape. The witness spoke to Tomo Batinic, a Serb, who was president of the Rogatica municipal Assembly. The witness asked Batinic what would happen to them. Batinic told the witness that it was too late, that everything would be destroyed. At the school, guards forced detainees to sign papers stating that they had voluntarily joined the Serbian Orthodox religion. The witness states that groups of men were sometimes taken out and brought behind the school. The witness would then hear shooting, and the men who had been taken away would not return. The witness states that about 30 men, three of whom were cousins of the witness, were removed from the camp under the orders of Rajko Kusic, and used as human shields. The witness heard that only two of the men survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm going to be asking you some questions on certain parts of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to be going serially through the statement and I will be directing Your Honours to the correct paragraph numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, for you it's not really necessary for you to consult your statement; I'll describe the context. In paragraph 9 of the witness's statement, sir, you said that after the multi-party elections, you spoke to your friend, Rajko Kusic, and he decided to leave his job, and you asked him why he was leaving. What was his response to that question?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: "Radovan pays me better."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did he explain who Radovan was?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Well, I knew, so I didn't ask which Radovan; the president of the SDS, the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to move now to the part of the witness's statement which deals with the distribution of arms to local Serbs, which is paragraph 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to that last portion, I understood that that last aspect was excised from the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is absolutely right, it was excised, and it was excised for this reason: That I was going to ask the witness to -- questions about that very excised portion, in accordance with the guidance which we've received as to the procedure to be followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm glad that's been clarified, Your Honour. I thought it had been excised for all purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could do the same; just first not to concentrate that much on the text of paragraph 14 but first listen to the testimony the witness elicits, and finally, if it is exactly the same, then of course it's -- but I see that in the original, which is in front of me, there's one portion deleted on page 3, second line, but 14 is still in, Mr. Gaynor. There are some other portions on page 8 deleted as well, redacted, but 14 is in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I might clarify the position. Where there is a statement which goes to a matter which is clearly -- well, frankly, which is fairly directly related to the Bosnian Serb leadership, that has been excised as that goes to the core of this case. Now, where there's a matter which is not of such critical importance, and I wish to ask the question -- the witness further questions about the matter, the -- there has been no excision; I'm going to ask the witness to expand on what's already in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just see if we need it as a point of reference in order to better understand the additional questions and we'll hear any further objections against keeping it in, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, I just wanted to clarify it because it's excised in the exhibit that's before the Court and I thought it was an excision for all purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not excised. Paragraph 14, you're talking about, is not excised in this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. I think she's referring to paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour. I'm referring to the evidence that was just given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, just given. Yes, I see that the last few words of paragraph 9 is, so I'm a bit confused. The last few words of paragraph 9 have been taken out.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, and that was the matter of which Mr. Gaynor just asked questions, reintroducing the material that was deleted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Hence the source of my intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I better understand because we're moving to 14 and now I better understand that we are back at 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Taking it out for reasons understandable under 92 bis and 89(F), of course, does not prevent the Prosecution from raising questions in relation to those parts which are less suitable for a 92 bis or 89(F) treatment but of course are still fully open for questioning from the witness as a viva voce witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, but I wanted to clarify that aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I thought they were being excised for all purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to direct Your Honours, as I said, to paragraph 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your statement, you've said that -- you describe a JNA military truck which came to your neighbourhood and parked near a community hall, and you say that the truck was filled with cases of weapons. My first question is did you personally see the truck yourself?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, why did you conclude that the cases which you saw were -- contained weapons? Why did you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Well, I came to that conclusion quite simply. It's a simple conclusion. They were driven in by army trucks. Second, there was security for -- provided by people carrying weapons and protecting this, and the circumstances and the situation in the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina and the information we would get from people who had fled from Visegrad, for example. They would let it be known that these were weapons, weapons that were stored in the centre, in the Dom. I didn't give it much thought, didn't think about why the weapons -- they were coming in, why

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to invite you to clearly state your answer because sometimes by nodding it's clear to us but then it does not appear on paper and it is not translated, so therefore could you give an explicit answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to direct you now to paragraph 19, which concerns some murders which took place before the shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps before you do so, I would have one question for the witness. Were you familiar with sizes of cases for weapons and could you say something more about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I can say is -- give you a rough estimate; there were large crates, large cases, perhaps two metres in length and one metre wide. There were smaller cases, medium cases, so different sized cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you say that you saw your neighbours take the weapons, were they then out of the cases or would they take such cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The neighbours I saw were already bearing weapons and they were taking up the cases from the trucks, off the trucks and taking them into the Dom, the centre across the road from the church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you did not see any weapons coming out of those cases.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at that point, no, while I was watching and all the times that I saw this, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Hanoteau also has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, what kind of neighbourhood Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was it? Where did you live, in what kind of neighbourhood? You're talking about your Serb neighbours. Were there any other neighbours in your neighbourhood belonging to another ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Turn it to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I direct Your Honours' attention to paragraph 19 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, in your written statement, you said that before the shelling of the town of Rogatica began, there were several murders in villages near Rogatica. Do you know the ethnicity of the murdered victims? Who was murdered?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: According to what people told me, this is information that reached town, these were people who were ethnic Muslims, I mean the persons who were killed, because Kusic and people who thought like him had already started acting like a Chetnik detachment or platoon -- I'm not very knowledgeable about these things. They were already active in this way in the villages around Rogatica where there was a Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Who do you believe murdered those Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: They were murdered by ethnic Serbs in uniform. The Serbs in Rogatica themselves at that time called them the Chetnik detachments, in uniforms of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, but they were saying that it was now the regular Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You said in your statement that as a result of those murders, people started to panic. Could you just clarify, which people started to panic?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Before this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- further proceeding with the questioning, I would just indicate, Your Honour, as a marker, that questions directed to belief without factual foundation are objected to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it was on my mind as well, I was a bit surprised. The witness did not answer what he believed but said what happened, although did not establish a -- at least, it was not clear on the basis of what he considered this to have happened. But I do agree with Ms. Loukas that asking what a witness believes is calling for speculation, but I'll allow you to further lay a factual foundation and the results.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, on what basis did you believe that those Muslims were murdered by ethnic Serbs in uniform? Why did you believe that?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: On the basis of statements made by people who lived in those villages and who saw Serb soldiers killing several persons, women included. The people who stated that were ethnic Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You said in your statement that as a result of those murders, people started to panic. Could you clarify which people you're referring to there.

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: I'm going to talk specifically about my family, about my street, about people who were near me. We were all together and these were people who were ethnic Muslims and also an elderly Croat lady. When this shelling took place in the neighbouring villages, she fled from there. I saw her in the street and I invited her to my house. She stayed with us for a while and I can say that from that moment onwards, there was absolute panic among people, absolute fear from the uncertain. So speaking in terms of percentage, Muslims accounted for a vast majority, and in my street, there was that Croat woman too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to move now to the portion of your statement dealing with the shelling of Rogatica town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is paragraphs 20 and 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, in your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement, you said that "Rogatica is in a valley and you could see the artillery positions surrounding us." Did you see those artillery positions with your naked eye?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And how far away were they?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: The closest artillery position was perhaps about 50 or 60 metres away from my house as the crow flies. That was a position within a factory compound. I even recognised the person who was operating the weapon. He was a Serb neighbour of mine and his garden was opposite mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you say that shelling came from the directions of certain areas?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Yes. I said that that was the closest one. And there was another one that was really nearby, another position from which firing came, and I saw the operations myself. Perhaps it's about 100 metres away as the crow flies. Again, I recognised the people manning the weapons. One of them actually went to elementary school with me. Those were the two closest artillery positions that I observed directly without any difficulty at all. Other artillery positions could be seen only when they were actually firing from there, when people could hear the sound and see the smoke. So from that side where I could see, I saw that in that part, Rogatica was completely surrounded by artillery weapons that were firing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to ask you a question, please. You say that the shelling began on the 21st or on the 22nd of May. Do you recall the time? When did it begin exactly?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm just concerned that the last answer may need to be redacted in terms of the protective nature of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that would be the next redaction. Yes, but first let's deal with the one that is already 15 minutes old and which, Mr. Registrar, if you need any guidance, then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, may I ask your attention for -- it's now the third redaction we have to make. We have to turn it to private session if there's any identifying element.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Certainly, I will be careful with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I think His Honour Judge Hanoteau was going to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, he was about to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to ask you, when did the shelling begin; do you recall the exact time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember it was 12.00 noon. I was in the street, in the main street in our town. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted). There was a lot of panic everywhere. We did not know who was shooting and from where. People tend to feel lost in situations like that. We just tried to get to our house where our children were. As for the time, it was 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know why the shelling began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm still trying to find an answer to that question why Rogatica was shelled, why the shelling started, and against whom this shelling was aimed at and why it lasted so long. As we started fleeing once the shelling began, people who stayed behind in Rogatica were the ones who actually started fleeing because it was only Muslims who stayed behind. Serb women and children had already been evacuated to Serbia, so it was clear against who these shells were and what their objective was, what their target was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But sir, before noon, in the morning, let's say, or during the night the previous night, was there shooting? Did you hear anything? Were there any attacks?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Not in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the next section, I think we should go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn it to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, after the shelling of Rogatica took place, did troops enter Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: I'm sorry, do you mean after the first shelling or after the shelling that by then was taking place every day? I don't really understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you tell us, in relation to the shelling, when the troops entered Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Now I understand the question. The town of Rogatica was shelled for a very long time. The formations that I've already mentioned entered the town gradually, cleaning up street after street, house after house, and that is how they approached the centre of town. So these military formations entered the town gradually. As far as I know, it went on for about two and a half months or three and a half months, until the entire town was cleansed of its Muslim Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. population and until it was fully taken over by Serb military formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When you say that the troops entered the town gradually, cleaning up street after street, what do you mean by the words "cleaning up"?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Clean-up in the war that I was in and that I'm testifying about now as a witness is the ugliest thing that a person could imagine. It means entering a street or a house -- perhaps it's best to explain it by way of the example of a house. Hand grenades are thrown on a house, the house is entered violently, by force, the door is broken down, automatic rifles, machine-guns are used, fired at the house mercilessly. If anybody were in the house, they'd be killed. Whoever would have the good fortune of not being killed, then they would be detained. Then the specialists would come in. They had flame throwers and that is how houses were set on fire. That is how house after house was dealt with, street after street, neighbourhood after neighbourhood until ultimately the entire town was destroyed. All the Muslim houses were torched. Many people, innocent people, civilians, women, children lost their lives. Many were brought to the Veljko Vlahovic school that had been turned into a detention centre. Others were brought to the place where weapons were unloaded. That is where they were detained. Others yet were taken to the elementary school and detained there. Then the fourth group was taken to a farm, to those barns of the farm that had been empty for years. The fifth group were taken to a factory and that is where they were detained. So the word "clean-up" is something inconceivable. For me, it is still inconceivable. So I think that I cannot paint a clearer picture for you than what I've said so far in terms of what "clean-up" meant in my books. It is an inhumane act. Unfortunately, in that war, it was an inhumane act committed by the Serbs against unarmed civilians in a town who had no intention of putting up any kind of resistance against Serb soldiers or our Serb neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, you referred in your --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just before the next question, and perhaps Mr. Gaynor will be proceeding to do this, just in relation to that, the last answer, it, I think, would be more useful to the Trial Chamber to know what is result of direct knowledge and what information is being conveyed on the basis of knowledge from others and hearsay and what have you, but I think perhaps Mr. Gaynor might be proceeding to do that. I just wanted to ensure that that was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, your attention is drawn to -- but perhaps it would be better at all to try to keep answers and questions closer together. I fully understand the witness wants to tell us a lot about -- I think you could tell us for days and days what happened. We are under time restraints so would you specifically focus on the questions asked to you by Mr. Gaynor and that perhaps would help. Please proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, in your answer, you said that many people were killed during the cleaning operation in Rogatica. Do you know how many people, approximately, were killed?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: I don't know the official figure. I don't know the official figure how many civilians in Rogatica were killed, lost their lives in that cleaning operation in Rogatica, but I do know that in my street, and in the next two streets which were inhabited by purely Muslim inhabitants, that within the space of one hour, 300 were killed, and at the very last minute, I managed to escape myself because I fled to the square where the majority of the population had already taken refuge because you have new buildings on the square that were fairly well protected, or rather, you could find shelter there in the basements or in those buildings, and that was our only salvation at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, in your previous answer, you referred to troops going from house to house. Did you personally see those troops or did you hear about that from other people?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Concretely speaking about my street and what happened in my street, I didn't have a chance of seeing this because I'd already left, but my former friend, acquaintance, who was a Serb soldier, told me about it in detail, and he named names.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You also referred to the killing of approximately 300 people. Do you remember what date, approximately, that took place?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: 19th of July, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And how did you hear about those killings?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: I heard about them, I said a moment ago that a Serb soldier told me about them. We knew each other. We'd known each other for a long time. We socialised. He came to the camp one day, called me, offered me a cigarette, and said he was sorry that my house had been destroyed during that operation. And by the by, he said he was happy that I had, as luck would have it, that I had been there and that I survived it all, that I was there. So that happened in the camp, that is to say, I received information in the camp what was done in my street and how many innocent women and children and men had fallen casualty.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to direct your attention to the last few sentences of paragraph 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement, you said that you heard several announcements by the Serbian army and Chetniks in Rogatica town and they were making announcements with a loudspeaker. The first question is where were these loudspeakers located?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: One was located right next to the secondary school centre in the northern part of town, the exit towards Sarajevo, and the second one was in the south, towards Visegrad, the road towards Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Why did you conclude that it was the Serbian army and Chetniks that were making announcements?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Well, because the announcements came from the command of the Serb army and the command that was led by Rajko Kusic, and it was common knowledge amongst us that Rajko Kusic was -- well, they asked us in the camp to refer to him as Vojvoda Rajko Kusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Why did you believe that the announcements were coming from the command of the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: On the basis of the fact that I think when the third announcement came, I directly had occasion to talk to Zivojin Novakovic who came up in a tank, escorted by Serb soldiers, and he personally read out to us the announcement once again without a loudspeaker, with instructions as to what we were supposed to do, and at a certain point during our talk, because I personally took part in that talk, conversation, he was told that in that part of town, the square where the new buildings were, that there were two and a half thousand, roughly, up to 3.000 women, children, and sick persons, men, civilians, and that the offer made to us by the Serb command couldn't be actually put into practice because so many people could not fit into the secondary school centre. The school wasn't big enough to take in all those people who were there. Then we asked that he should try and talk to the command and -- I'll have to paraphrase here, I can't remember every single word, but I and another man, an elderly man, and we were there directly, next to Zivojin, said that there was so many people on the square, 2.500 to 3.000 civilians, as I said, and that we said to him, "Bring the Serb flag, fly the Serb flag. If we recognise the Serb Republic and the authorities and the laws and everything you want, just stop the shelling. We can't all fit into the school building, there are too many of us." And he said, "All right, I'll do the best I can and talk to the command." He got into the tank and went off. He left, and then afterwards he said -- he came back and he said he had talked to them but nothing would come of that. "You nevertheless all have to go to the secondary school centre, to the school building in order to avoid -" that's what he said - "to avoid the cleaning."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next main area concerns the school. I don't know when Your Honours wish to take a break

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had in mind to take a break in a couple of minutes, but we could do it now and then restart at ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that, caused by the many redactions we had to make, unfortunately, that we have to break for 30 minutes. That means that we'll restart at five minutes to 1.00 sharp, this clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If any of the parties would ask me what "sharp" means, I had to admit that it was on the side of the Chamber that the discipline was lacking. Please proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're still in open session, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The next part of this examination will concern the school and that really starts at around paragraph 26 of the witness's statement, at page 5, and continues for the next couple of pages. I'd like the witness to be shown the next exhibit, please, and I'd request that the exhibit be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P578.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the buildings on that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Well, they are photographs of the secondary school centre called Veljko Vlahovic in Rogatica. They are photographs of buildings, the buildings in which I spent about three and a half months as a detainee with my family and with many other civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. You can put that exhibit to one side, sir. Now, did you go to this school in order to seek refuge? Did you find it a place of refuge?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Whenever they used the loudspeaker system to make an announcement and -- in which they said that the Muslims could take refuge in the school building, the Veljko Vlahovic secondary school centre, they also said that in that school, in the school building, which, as they said, we were supposed to stay for two to three days until the town had been cleaned up, that we would be protected from the effects of the war, that there would be no shooting, that they wouldn't shoot at us, that we wouldn't have any problems, that we would just avoid the war operations going on in town if we took refuge for two or three days in the school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in your statement - and I'll direct Their Honours to paragraph 27 - you say that you concluded that it was a concentration camp. What was it that brought you to conclude that it was a concentration camp?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Well, as soon as I arrived at the school after the first two or three days when we were told it was the time we would spend there, and they said that if we had any food, we should take it with us to keep us going during those two, three days, so nothing actually happened during the first two or three days which would allow us to conclude that it was anything else but what they announced that it was. However, on the third day, we, or rather, I came to the conclusion that something was amiss, that something was wrong, and that I couldn't recognise in what was around me what they had said that we would come across because the Serb police would storm the building, people I didn't know would enter. They were in uniform with weapons. And these people engaged in negative actions against the people in the school and those who had tried to save their families and their own lives in taking refuge from the war operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Were you permitted to leave -- to enter and exit the school at will?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: No, we were prohibited from leaving the school, and to the right of the entrance into the school, to the right-hand side, nearby there was the administration offices of the transport company in Rogatica. And on the roof of that company, there was a machine-gun nest which we could see every day. There was soldiers there in the sniper's nest and around the buildings, near the school building. At the entrance itself, the doors were fastened with thick chain. To the left of the school, there was another machine-gun nest manned with soldiers, and we were warned that the whole area around the school had been mined, in fact, and that if anybody attempted to flee or jump out of a window from one of the school classrooms, that would be impossible because the whole area around was mined. Mines had been laid and there were guards on duty around the school, so that was the situation. You weren't able to leave, nor did you dare leave, and of course you were prohibited from leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Approximately how often did you receive meals while you were detained at the school?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Well, we ate the rations we had brought in ourselves very quickly, we got through them very quickly, and then the real trouble started with respect to food because there were many women and children there and they had nothing to eat. Nobody had any food left. There were -- we didn't have anything to eat for days, then on other days, the Serb army would turn up, Serb soldiers would turn up with a small truck and they would bring in five or six sacks of potatoes, for example, several bottles of cooking oil, some pasta, or something like that. So that was -- those were the foodstuffs that we were given. That was the kind of food that we were given by the Serb army, a little flour, perhaps, very little. For example, in one of these -- in one of these instances where they brought in some food, my family received three potatoes, three or four thin bits of pasta, and the line I was waiting in, the cooking oil had -- there wasn't enough to go around, so we didn't get any. So this was for -- in the period of, say, 21 days, they would bring in these rations when they brought in a large group of women and children and men. Then they would bring in, later on, some of this food which wasn't enough, not only for the people that they had brought in but certainly not for the people who were already there, to go around. There were water shortages, there was very little water to be had because the main water supply line, due to the tank operations near the school building, as the soil was soft, the tank fell through the ground and damaged the water supply lines, pipes, so the water situation was very difficult, very short supply of water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, I foresee that you will be in time trouble rather soon. Could you please try to get a bit more control. Of course it's important to know whether there was sufficient water or not, but if there was insufficient water, whether it was due to broken pipelines, due to failing trucks, transport, is really not something ... I'm asking, Mr. Gaynor, to put the questions more specifically to you, because for this Chamber, of course if there is any specific reason why one day there was no water, we'd like to know, but in general, if you say there was not sufficient water, then we are inclined to accept that. And if there's any doubt on that, you will certainly get some questions from the Defence which would then put that into question. A bit of tighter control, Mr. Gaynor, would really be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Certainly, I will certainly do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very briefly, sir, could you describe very briefly, how often did you wash yourself during your three and a half months at the school?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: I managed just once, the upper half of my body, my torso.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And in the rooms in which you slept, how many people slept in the rooms in which you slept?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: It depended. In my room, in the room I was in, there were 47 of us, including women, children, adults.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in paragraph 29 of your statement, you said that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. shortly after you arrived at the camp, you were brought to see Rajko Kusic. And you describe him as the commander of the camp. Why do you describe him as the commander of the camp?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Because in talking to him, he personally told me that he was the commander of the town of Rogatica, that he was the commander of the camp, and that in fact that everything was under his auspices or leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, you've said that the camp grew to hold 1.100 people. To the best of your knowledge, what ethnicity were those people, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: All the people there were Muslims except for two women who were Serbs but married to Muslims, and they were with us the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd request that the witness now be shown the next exhibit, please, and I'd request an exhibit number for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P579.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This exhibit which is being sent around now is named Serbian Army of BH Rogatica Brigade Command. It's dated at Borika the 11th of June, 1992, it's directed to the SRK command, and it's signed by Commander Rajko Kusic, and it also bears a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you concentrate yourself on the first paragraph of this document, you'll see in the brigade's zone of responsibility, there were no sizeable enemy activities. Now, is that consistent with what you observed in Rogatica during this period, which is June 1992?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, if he says it's not consistent, that's of course the answer you could expect. If you do not clearly say that this is an SRK, so the enemy of the SRK would be Muslims, and therefore you should put that in context in order to get the answer, at least I expect, you would like to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask it to the witness. This is a report in which the Serb army says that there were no sizeable enemy activities, that is, enemies of the Serbs, let's say Croats or Muslims. Is that consistent with your observations, that the enemies of the Serbs had no sizeable activities? That means Croats, Muslims, whoever had forces there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. We were civilians without weapons so we were in the hands of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, very briefly, Witness, the last sentence in that paragraph says, "The people are finding shelter in the secondary school centre." Could you just confirm that the expression "finding shelter" is an inaccurate statement of what those people were doing in that school.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that question, of course, is posed in a thoroughly objectionable form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not only that but the question has already been put and answered by the witness, so there's no -- I mean, it's clear that what is described here does not fit at all in the description the witness has given before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you very much. I'll move on. At this point, Witness -- I'd just like to point out to Your Honours a typographical error at paragraph 31 of the English statement of this witness. This typo does not appear in the B/C/S version of the statement. On the third line at the end, it says maybe 300 hundred people, which suggests 30.000, Your Honours can strike the word "hundred" because the correct number is 300.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your statement you said that 300 people were getting on to trucks in the school compound to leave Rogatica. My question is this: Were those people voluntarily leaving Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, that question can be posed in a less leading form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may answer the question. Sir, the question was whether these 300 people on the trucks, whether they were voluntarily leaving Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we'll move directly into private session at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, since the public gallery was, with my consent, not entirely empty - I think it is now - we are in private session and the public gallery is empty now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not confirmed on my screen yet, Mr. Gaynor. Now it is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We're now going to be dealing with a description of events at paragraph 37 of the witness's statement, which is page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement you refer to Tomo Batinic. Do you know his full first name?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Tomislav Batinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now request that the next exhibit be distributed and that it be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I understand this has an exhibit number; it is P64.A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there's no need to assign any other number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This document is headed Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Presidency, it's dated Pale, 20th of July, 1992. It's signed by the president of the Presidency, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, and it bears a stamp. It lists the members of the War Commission for the Serbian municipality of Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: At number 2, Witness, you see Tomislav Batinic. Do you believe that to be the Tomo Batinic who you spoke to in the camp?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you see the name Sveto Vaselinovic?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Sveto was president of the SDS in the town of Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your -- in your document you also see the name of Milorad Sokolovic. Now, in your statement at paragraph 14, you said that you saw a Mile Sokolovic distributing weapons, and you later clarified that that was Milorad Sokolovic. Do you believe that person could be the same person as listed on this document?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Yes, because we all called Milorad Sokolovic "Mile," and I know for sure that it's one and the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement - this is paragraph 37, Your Honours - you say that in your conversation with Tomo Batinic, he told you that it was too late, everything will be destroyed. What did you understand him to mean by those words?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: My understanding was that nothing could be helped, that no one could hope to survive any longer. It was said that all the prisoners at the school would disappear and that it was too late for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Who said that all the prisoners at the school would disappear?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Well, Tomislav Batinic did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to the next topic. There's no need for you to look at that exhibit anymore, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question, Witness 382. You said Mr. Batinic said that all Muslims would disappear. Did you understand this to be disappear at all, or to disappear from the territory of Rogatica, or any other way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My understanding was that we'd all be killed there, that we'd be killed, because before that conversation, many people had been killed. They disappeared from the camp. They were executed. All of us who were still there at the time were told that we'd all be killed, that we'd all disappear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The next subject is forced labour, and that is mentioned in paragraph 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement, you said that your son was forced to work as a forced labourer. Has your son told you what kind of labour he carried out?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: They were digging trenches for the Serb army, they carried ammunition, they made machine-gun nests out of sandbags, they buried corpses in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did your son describe any mistreatment that he received while he was carrying out those tasks?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Yes. Every time when he'd come back, he'd tell me that if you didn't work fast enough or if you didn't do exactly what they said, they would beat you, swear at you, insult you, threaten to kill you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How old was your son at that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Thirteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to refer Your Honours to paragraph 40 on page 7 of the ICTY statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement, you said there was a time when Macola was the commander of the camp and Rajko Kusic was the commander of the town. Now --

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, why do you describe Macola as the commander of the camp? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: Because one day a Serb soldier in uniform appeared in the classroom where I was and he introduced himself not by name, he introduced himself as a Serb soldier who had come from the front in Serb Krajina in Croatia, that he was now the new commander of our camp, that we should be obedient from every conceivable point of view, that we should carry out his orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Witness 382
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When you say that Macola was the commander of the camp and Kusic was the commander of the town, does that mean that Kusic no longer had any control over the camp?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In what respect did change the position of Mr. Kusic, if at all, due to Mr. Macola being the new camp commander in relation to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kusic was followed up as a camp commander by Mr. Macola. Not being the commander, was his position in relation to the camp nil, was there still any relation left, him not being the camp commander anymore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because he was the absolute commander. Being camp commander meant that he was subordinated to the chief commander, that was Rajko Kusic. Truth to tell, he didn't appear that much later, he would appear at night. But I do not see that he particularly lost any responsibility, in view of what was going on in the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now, Your Honours I'm going to ask some questions relating to paragraph 47 which is at the very bottom of page 7 and the top of page 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Looking at the clock, Mr. Gaynor, do you think that we -- you would finish within a couple of minutes the examination-in-chief or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that I will not be finished in the next couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then before entering into a new area, perhaps we could use the last two minutes to see what the remainder of the week will be for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because we are two minutes from the break. Witness 382, we will stop for the day. We'd like you to come back tomorrow in the morning. I take it that we'll conclude also by tomorrow. I have to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony you have given until now or the testimony you are still about to give. Perhaps for your personal guidance, knowing that you're -- perhaps I go in private session for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Very practical, Mr. Gaynor; how much time would you still need? I've seen estimates of four hours, of three hours, and the four hours at least was accompanied by a considerable gain of time due to 89(F).

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I won't proceed for more than 45 minutes tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What, then, have we gained on 89(F)?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the case of this specific witness, he did have quite a lot of extra information. I'll revise my estimate, I'll work on it overnight, and I'll compress it to 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before I say yes or no, my next question would be, Ms. Loukas, how much time would you need to cross-examine Witness 458? I'm asking this because sometimes the Chamber is surprised by the time taken or not taken to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'll take that on board, Your Honour. Just in relation to Witness 458, being the fourth witness this week --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I should first have asked about cross-examination of Witness 382, but if you deal with them together.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. Well, firstly, in relation to Witness 382, I would have thought an hour would see me out easily. That's my estimate at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would bring us, half an hour and an hour, to the first break tomorrow morning, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we start even more sharp than we did today, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. The other witness, of course, is Witness 458 and -- the fourth witness this week, and I can indicate that I will have something of a reprieve in that, having done the first three witnesses, Mr. Stewart will be doing witness number four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So I haven't, at this stage, consulted with Mr. Stewart to see how long he thinks cross-examination might take. That witness, of course, is the witness relating to the Banja Luka municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that. If, of course, we could finish with that witness in the two and a half hours remaining, then that would be good, for the witness also.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. Of course the -- keeping witnesses here over the weekend is something ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we do agree that we'll try to fill the programme tomorrow that would suit both the needs of the witness. Perhaps also for the Prosecution -- of course in my view and in the view of the Chamber, it takes a lot of time. First of all, better control of the witnesses is really needed. We saw it immediately after you changed the way of examining the witness and it gave just as much relevant information you were seeking. That's one. But there are other matters as well. For example, I have now seen two pictures of a school building. That's fine if there would be any dispute about whether this was the school building, but I do not take that that's the case. I have seen in my life some 100 or 200, 500 school buildings, I have an impression, so unless there's any specific reason why the layout of that school building would add anything to the information about people being detained in school buildings, we do without. This is just one example but I'd like the parties to think about the relevance of these matters at all details because it will save us at least 25 or 30 per cent of our time. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 1st day of April, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1:51 p.m.
